extracted.intended_audience: Coast Guard contracting officers, procurement officials, policy analysts, and researchers studying OMB A-76 commercial activity contracting
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and practical guidance for implementing, writing, administering, and evaluating Coast Guard commercial-activity contracts under OMB Circular A-76, including PWS development, cost comparison to a Most Efficient Organization (MEO), and causes of contract cost increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance Work Statement (PWS) comprehensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the Performance Work Statement (PWS) specifies exactly what is required under the contract, the thesis will also examine PWS deficiencies that may have contributed to cost increases after contractor performance begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PWS must be accurate and comprehensively describe all the work which the function performs; omissions can lead to contract modifications and cost growth. Thorough study of the function and quick but careful analysis of tasks are required when writing the PWS.

rubrics_metrics.name: PWS clarity and conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: To be effective, the PWS would also need to be written clearly and concisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, concise writing reduces misinterpretation by contractors and administration problems. Rushed or unclearly written PWSs (due to schedule pressure) increase the risk of omissions and later disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: PWS work categorization: Standing vs Unscheduled Work
rubrics_metrics.description: Work which the function performs was broken down into: Standing, or Scheduled Work, and Unscheduled Work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standing/Scheduled Work is recurrent and can be planned in advance (usually specified with frequency). Unscheduled Work (repairs, installations, modifications) cannot be accurately planned but is expected to occur over the life of the function—both must be identified in the PWS.

rubrics_metrics.name: PWS pricing/work levels: Level I, II, III
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing Work is Level I (quantified at a fixed price). Level II Work includes repairs up to $25,000 (quantified at a fixed price). Level III Work is all other Unscheduled Work (negotiated as performance dictates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PWS should quantify Level I and II work where possible and provide adequate historical data about frequency/amounts of Level II/III to allow offerors to price realistically; failure to do so leads to later contract modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: PWS must provide accurate historical data
rubrics_metrics.description: Finally, the PWS must provide accurate historical data. This affords potential bidders some idea of the nature and frequency of Level II and Level III Work to be expected, and gives them the basis for developing their price proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without reliable historical data bidders under- or over-price risks, leading to later contract adjustments or contractor claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management Study / MEO development
rubrics_metrics.description: From the PWS, the Government then determined the best organizational structure, staffing, and operating procedures for what was defined as the Most Efficient Organization (MEO). Following this, the costs of operating the function under the MEO were developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper Management Study should produce an MEO based on the PWS; inadequately trained personnel or lack of technical assistance produces weak MEOs and flawed cost comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personnel qualifications for PWS/Management Study authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally, personnel thoroughly familiar with A-76 should have been assigned to each unit for the express purpose of conducting the Management Study and developing the PWS. Unfortunately, no such personnel were made available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trained staff or provide technical assistance; relying on inadequately trained unit personnel leads to late PWS development, incomplete PWS content, and delayed contracting decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Invitation For Bid (IFB) when Government is a bidder
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the functions contracted out, all contracts awarded competitively were solicited as Invitations For Bid (IFB). This was done because the Government was also a bidder based on the MEO, and would have had an unfair advantage in a negotiated contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When government (MEO) competes, use IFB procurement methods to preserve fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wholesale adaptation of clauses from other services
rubrics_metrics.description: To save time, the schedule and contract clauses of the IFB were adapted to Department of Transportation/Coast Guard requirements from an Air Force housing maintenance contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapting clauses from other services may introduce mismatches with DOT/Coast Guard needs; ensure clauses reflect the operating agency's requirements to prevent misinterpretation and administration issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract definitions must be clear (e.g., appliances vs equipment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The contract definition of 'appliances' and 'equipment' is not clear. The contract does state that an appliance which become unserviceable will be replaced by the Government, while equipment which becomes unserviceable will be replaced by the contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous definitions lead to unresolved contractor-government disputes and delayed clarifications (e.g., water heaters). Define key terms explicitly in the PWS/IFB and respond promptly to contractor queries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation and training of Contracting Officer's Technical Representatives (COTRs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The COTR has generally given the contractor a second chance to make corrections. None of the three interviewed for this thesis had received any training other than on-the-job training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COTRs should be designated in writing and receive proper formal training; untrained or undesignated COTRs increase risk of inconsistent oversight, unofficial interpretations, and administration problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include deduct provisions/incentives in firm fixed price contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: As the contract is written, there is no method to take deductions for sub-standard performance. Including deduct provisions provides a means for the Contracting Officer to get the attention of a substandard performer to make improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add explicit deduct or incentive clauses to manage contractor performance; relying solely on goodwill or second chances reduces Government leverage against poor performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract administration: ACO familiarity and responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The COTR and Housing Officer identified a lack of administrative contract support from the Administrative Contracting Officer (ACO). The current ACO has never visited the site. Contract interpretations either are subject to inordinate delays, or are never received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACO should be familiar with the contract, conduct site visits, and provide timely interpretations. Centralized or remote administration without regular site engagement harms contract performance and increases disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and accountability for Government Furnished Equipment/Material (GFE/GFM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control over Government Furnished Equipment (GFE) is lacking. Tools used by the former Government organization were made available to the contractor. However, there was no corresponding system to maintain accountability of these items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain inventories and accountability systems for GFE/GFM at transition and during performance to prevent misappropriation, schedule impacts, and cost disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary causes of contract cost increases
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on the data gathered from three Coast Guard commercial activity functions, the primary reason for cost increases are wage increases from Department of Labor Wage Determination Adjustments. In only one instance, cost increases were attributable to increases in the scope of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect contract modifications for wage-determination driven adjustments; evaluate contract terms and pricing strategies to anticipate DOL wage impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other causes of cost increases: additional work and authorized wage increases
rubrics_metrics.description: General Accounting Office found that 'cost increases resulted primarily from additional work and authorized wage increases.' The Service Contract Act requires contractors to pay not less than prevailing minimum wage as determined by DOL; contractor bids and in-house estimates do not include costs for future wage increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing bids or comparing costs, account for the likelihood of future wage determinations and scope changes; consider contract clauses and contingencies to manage these risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of delivery delays for GFE/GFM
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery of GFE and Government Furnished Material (GFM) is difficult to plan for; long transit times (e.g., to Hawaii) take a long time from order to arrival. Late arrival causes schedule slippages, which can result in cost increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan logistics lead times for GFE/GFM in the PWS and include contingencies for delivery delays to reduce schedule-driven cost growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define government-side roles and authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The responsibilities of the Housing Officer, the assistant Housing Officer, and the COTR have not been clearly defined to the contractor. They have been tasked by various members of the Housing Office, but weren't sure if that person actually had the authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify individual responsibilities and lines of authority in writing in the contract administration documents to reduce confusion and disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost comparison methodology (contractor vs MEO)
rubrics_metrics.description: To make the comparison, a hypothetical Government organization was developed, based on the MEO or the Government workforce in existence at the time the function was turned over to the contractor. The cost of the hypothetical Government organization was calculated using the current Federal General Services pay scale for GS-classified billets or the current local Wage Grade pay scale for WG-classified billets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert WG hourly rates to yearly salary using 2,037 hours per year. For military billets, calculate equivalent pay including retirement (~29.15% of base pay) and FICA (~7.15%), and include BAQ and BAS for officers. Apply these conversions consistently when comparing contract price to government performance cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government disadvantage on recompetition: 25% capital improvement increase
rubrics_metrics.description: Second, the government estimate would automatically be increased by 25-percent for capital improvement. In re-competing a function, the Government is at a distinct disadvantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that MEO/government cost estimates include a presumed 25% capital improvement factor when re-competing, which tends to bias recompetition decisions in favor of contractor performance; account for this in policy analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include specific, uncommon requirements in PWS (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for special services (e.g., having meals served to official party at their tables rather than subject them to standing in the chow line) are being accommodated though not specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include known special or ceremonial service requirements in the PWS so future contractors can plan and price for them; omission causes unplanned effort and potential cost increases or service shortfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of CA complexity when selecting cases for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the degree to which a CA's complexity may influence cost increases, the analysis consisted of relatively complex, moderately complex, and relatively simple CAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing cost behavior or selecting functions for A-76 review, classify functions by complexity (mix of standing vs unscheduled work) because complexity influences contract performance, modification frequency, and cost growth risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: study full effects of contracting out
rubrics_metrics.description: The Coast Guard should conduct a study to determine the full impact of contracting out functions under A-76. The effects of reduced flexibility, loss of opportunities for shore rotational tours, loss of training opportunities, and other negative impacts are unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions to contract out should weigh non-monetary impacts (flexibility, training, personnel management) as well as monetary savings; commission comprehensive impact studies before wide-scale contracting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: better contract administration resourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Maintenance and Logistics Command (MLC), Pacific, should provide better contract administration, especially in the area of contract interpretation. The office would benefit by the addition of another Contracting Officer billet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure contracting offices are staffed adequately to conduct site visits, respond to contractor queries, and manage modifications timely to prevent administrative delays that increase costs or diminish performance.
